summary: Defines terminology and design goals for autonomic networking, in which network functions self-configure, self-optimize, self-heal and self-protect with minimal human or central intervention. It sets the vocabulary for later work.

plainLanguage.summary: Autonomic networking aims to let network functions configure, adapt, and protect themselves with little detailed human input. This memo defines the terms and goals while explaining that operators and central guidance still have roles.

questions: what is the autonomic control plane
subtitle: Definitions and design goals for network functions that manage themselves with limited detailed configuration.

tldr.problem: Detailed, device-by-device network configuration can create dependencies on administrators or centralized management systems.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines autonomic behavior and Intent, then sets goals for self-management, security, distribution, reporting, shared infrastructure, and life-cycle support.
tldr.outcome: It provides common terminology and design goals, while stating that autonomic networking does not eliminate human operators or central control.

sections.title: Autonomic Versus Automatic
sections.content:
The memo focuses on node-level autonomic functions that reduce dependence on human administrators and central management systems. Such functions can exchange information with other nodes to create feedback loops. The four commonly cited properties are self-configuration, self-healing, self-optimization, and self-protection.

The document distinguishes autonomic behavior from an automatic process. An automatic process follows a sequence of rules chosen in advance and may need adjustment when conditions change. An autonomic function can adapt to a changing environment using self-knowledge, discovery, or high-level guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: An automatic process follows steps selected in advance. An autonomic function can use information about changing conditions to adjust its behavior.

sections.title: Intent, Domains, and Nodes
sections.content:
Intent is an abstract, high-level policy for operating an autonomic domain. It does not specify configuration for a particular node, though it may describe a role or function. An autonomic domain is a collection of nodes that use the same Intent.

An autonomic function needs no configuration to operate and can get required information through self-knowledge, discovery, or Intent. An Autonomic Service Agent implements all or part of such a function on an autonomic node. The memo defines an autonomic node as a node that requires no configuration, while allowing configuration to override an autonomic function.
sections.plainLanguage: Intent states a network-wide goal rather than a device-by-device command. Nodes in a domain use the same Intent, and service agents implement autonomic functions on those nodes.

sections.title: Design Goals and Coexistence
sections.content:
The design goals include self-management, secure-by-default interactions, decentralization, simple high-level interfaces, abstraction, reporting, common infrastructure, independence from any particular network layer, and support for a device's full life cycle. Autonomic systems should coexist with traditional management methods.

Management methods have a priority order: node-specific management takes precedence over autonomic Intent, and Intent takes precedence over autonomic default behavior. This preserves an administrator's ability to override network-wide behavior. The memo also suggests that unexpected conditions should not generally cause autonomic functions to switch off.
sections.plainLanguage: Autonomic functions should work securely and with limited central dependence, while still fitting into existing management. An administrator's node-specific settings can override Intent and default behavior.

sections.title: What Autonomic Networking Does Not Remove
sections.content:
Eliminating human operators is not a design goal. Autonomic networking aims to reduce tedious detailed work so operators can focus on oversight, policy, diagnosis, and responding to unusual situations.

Emergency fixes are also not eliminated; hardware failures and conditions an algorithm cannot handle may still require direct intervention. Nor is eliminating central control a goal. The memo instead describes central guidance at a higher abstraction level, such as Intent, rather than detailed commands for every device.
sections.plainLanguage: People still set policy, oversee the network, and handle problems that automated functions cannot resolve. The goal is to reduce repetitive configuration work, not remove human responsibility.

sections.title: The Autonomic Reference Model
sections.content:
An Autonomic Network consists of autonomic nodes that communicate through an Autonomic Control Plane. The control plane is intended to be secure and self-organizing. A node contains Autonomic Service Agents, self-knowledge, network discovery, and feedback-loop functions, along with an Autonomic User Agent for reporting to administrators.

The control plane carries functions such as Intent distribution, feedback, and discovery. The memo allows it to run in-band, over a configured VPN, over a self-managing overlay, or over a traditional out-of-band network. The document presents a high-level reference model and says further detail was still being developed when it was finalized.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node has service agents and information about itself, and can discover information about its network. A secure control plane lets autonomic nodes communicate and supports reporting to users.
